title: TESA — Telerobotic Endovascular Skills Assessment
tagline: Endovascular robotics · Open data and hardware
summary: An open-source guidewire robot and standardized dataset for endovascular navigation, contributed to the Open-H Endoluminal initiative.
body: Endovascular procedures such as mechanical thrombectomy depend on navigating flexible guidewires and catheters through intricate vascular networks. Modern soft-body physics simulators do not capture the edge cases or interaction dynamics these tools actually exhibit — the bending, buckling and torsion that accumulate under sustained torque and mechanical stress over many episodes.

TESA addresses that gap by collecting real-world data across a series of physical environments, or "gyms", spanning target poses from straightforward to nearly impossible. The lab is contributing two things to the Open-H Endoluminal ecosystem: a standardized endoluminal dataset (TESA-Data) and a low-cost open-source hardware platform (TESA-Bot). The model is the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery tasks, whose inexpensive standardized hardware reshaped the science of surgical skill assessment — we want the same for endovascular skills.

The platform pairs a two-degree-of-freedom guidewire and catheter driver with synchronized motor telemetry and an overhead camera that stands in for a single-plane fluoroscopy view. A set of 3D-printed vascular phantoms — some abstract bifurcations and aneurysms, others projections of real anatomy — is backlit so the guidewire can be tracked optically inside the channels. Data collection is driven largely by a reinforcement learning agent navigating the gyms in real time, with human operators covering the geometry it cannot reach.

Because every experiment runs on benchtop phantoms derived from open anatomical models, the dataset carries no HIPAA or PHI constraints. Everything generated under the project — software, firmware, CAD, schematics, recordings and metadata — is committed for public release under the OpenMDW-1.1 (Open Medical Data & Hardware) license.
researchers: Neev Zeroni, Tarun Sehgal, Sam Fisher, Gabriel Garso, Amit Manicka, Timothy M. Kowalewski
